title: Week 3 latency blitz POC sync
summary: Third weekly check-in for the HearthFin POC focused on reducing TTFT and stabilizing streaming tails. Reviewed last week's benchmark spreadsheet, validated early kernel swap gains on dev cluster, flagged a seqlen distribution mismatch, and agreed on a short list of next changes: tighten prefix cache, increase KV cache retention for common prompts, try a 4-bit quantized variant on a small shard, and run a 6-hour microburst sim. Action owners and targets captured below.
topics: kernel choices and hedging on e.g., fwd-optimized vs kernel-batch path
KV/prefix cache TTL and batching tradeoffs
security note: audit log retention and SSO mapping
action_items: Maya Chen (Redwood SE): generate microburst test plan + JMeter script, due 2026-01-22
Mark Dawson (HearthFin ML Eng): share real request seqlen histogram (last 7d) and top 50 prompt prefixes, due 2026-01-21
Ethan Brooks (AE): send updated pricing for 100k tokens/day pilot + dedicated burst option, due 2026-01-20
Lina Ortega (SRE): provision test VPC peering & share firewall rules for performance runs, due 2026-01-23
next_steps: Run 6-hour microburst sim Thursday 01/22 in staging with KV cache retention + 4-bit quantized variant
SE to upload updated benchmark sheet (v3) with per-kernel TTFT bootstraps
AE to schedule an on-site exec summary if microburst shows >20% TTFT improvement
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-19 15:00 PT | Duration: 46 minutes | Recording: yes | Join link: (redacted)
Attendees: Ethan, Maya (Redwood); Ravi, Lina, Mark (HearthFin)
---
[00:00] Ethan Brooks: Alright team, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — hit the new microbench results, dig into the streaming tail we saw, and lock owners for the microburst run. Maya you driving benchmarks today?
[00:28] Maya Chen: Yep, I pulled v2 of the bench sheet, link in chat, it's the one with per-kernel TTFT rows. Quick note — the dev cluster run swapped to the fwd-opt kernel at 50% routing and we saw a 11 to 16 percent TTFT drop on short prompts, but a small tail increase on 2% of requests.
[00:54] Ravi Kumar: When you say tail increase, is that p50 or p99? p50 is fine but p99 worries product.
[01:02] Maya Chen: Mostly p95+p99, so the long tail gets a bit worse — my guess is kernel warmup and microbatching timing. Might be sequence length skew; our profiling shows the fwd-opt path pays off for seqlen < 128.
[01:22] Mark Dawson: We actually have a big chunk of requests around 160 from our chatbot prompts — so that explains the mismatch. We can share histograms.
[01:32] Ethan Brooks: Great, Mark can you drop the seqlen histogram in the shared sheet after the call? That'll help Maya pick the right kernel route.
[01:40] Mark Dawson: Yep, I'll add it. Also curious about quant — did you try the 4-bit variant you mentioned last week?
[01:47] Maya Chen: We did a tiny shard test, not full production safe. 4-bit gave slightly faster decode, but TF dropping was inconsistent on longer sequences — something with GEMM precision and the KV alignment. Also the transcriber here might show it as 4 bit quiet like "for bit" in the sheet.
[02:08] Lina Ortega: From infra side we care about connection churn during streaming — we've seen a few dropped SSE connections at high concurrency. Anything we need to tweak on keepalives?
[02:18] Maya Chen: We saw keepalive intervals re-negotiating when prefix cache expired mid-stream. Increasing KV/prefix TTL reduced reconnects in sim.
[02:28] Ravi Kumar: Is that safe for memory? We have limited GPU RAM on staging.
[02:33] Maya Chen: TTL tuning is a trade — longer retention increases KV usage, but reduces average compute per request. We recommended TTL 60s for hot prefixes in the doc but can tune per workload.
[02:45] Ethan Brooks: Can we run a microburst sim that reproduces our on-call pattern? Maya, you said you'd script JMeter-like workload.
[02:55] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll push the script. Plan: 6h run, 15m ramps, three 2m bursts to 800rps to stress the streaming handshake and kernel hedging.
[03:10] Mark Dawson: I want us to include a path that forces hedging to fallback kernel, e.g., force route to kernel A, then on queue surge flip to kernel B, to see the state migration cost.
[03:24] Maya Chen: We'll instrument with per-request trace ids so we can see KV cache hits/misses and any extra latency from switching.
[03:32] Ravi Kumar: Security quick Q — audit logs retention, we're SOC2 aligned. How do we get the logs into our SIEM?
[03:41] Ethan Brooks: Redwood can stream audit events to their S3 or to a customer syslog endpoint; we also support pushing to Splunk/Datadog. I'll share the SOC2 + audit log playbook.
[03:53] Lina Ortega: And SSO? We need SAML mapping for RBAC.
[04:00] Ethan Brooks: We support SAML2.0, SCIM for provisioning. I'll loop in our security docs link.
[04:08] Maya Chen: Back to perf — one anomaly: on one run the pod cold start added ~120ms to TTFT probabilistically. Could be kernel loading overhead when eviction happens.
[04:21] Mark Dawson: That might be because our batching window is small. We have 8ms batching target on the agent side to keep lat low.
[04:30] Maya Chen: Right; there's a brittle point where batching + kernel load interacts. We can try pre-warming kernels on the dedicated pool during bursts.
[04:40] Ravi Kumar: Pre-warming costs us but could be worth it for peak SLAs. Are there econ numbers?
[04:46] Ethan Brooks: I'll include pricing options for pre-warm capacity in the update — different tiers: ephemeral burst units vs reserved.
[04:52] Mark Dawson: About the seqlen mismatch, when we shared our prompt prefixes — a majority are templated with user history included which bumps seqlen. Could we do smarter prefix caching keyed to the template hash rather than full prefix?
[05:09] Maya Chen: We do support prefix hashing; it's in the Optimize suggestions. Hashing the stable part of the prefix helps keep cache cardinality down. We'll recommend that in the bench doc.
[05:20] Ravi Kumar: Any concerns about quantization for legal/regulatory outputs? Our product needs determinism for some flows.
[05:28] Maya Chen: Quantization can change logits slightly, so for deterministic required flows we'd suggest using a higher-precision serving variant or pinning to a validated model version. But you can still use quantized for non-deterministic assistant channels.
[05:42] Lina Ortega: Okay. For the microburst we need firewall peering — I'll provision and share IP ranges.
[05:49] Ethan Brooks: Thanks Lina. Can you aim for 01/23 to have that ready?
[05:54] Lina Ortega: Yes.
[06:00] [short silence and screenshare noise]
[06:10] Maya Chen: I want to call out one odd metric — KV cache hit rate dropped during one of the ramp periods to 42% from 86%. The top prefixes were being evicted. That lines up with the reconnect pattern.
[06:22] Mark Dawson: If we increase the hot-TTL, does memory pressure spike linearly? We only have 24GB usable on the node.
[06:30] Maya Chen: We'll run a memory model in the next run. For now I'd recommend a conservative TTL bump to 30s and measure.
[06:39] Ethan Brooks: Does the team want a canary that only hedges 20% of traffic initially? That could limit risk.
[06:45] Ravi Kumar: Yes canarying is good. Start small.
[06:48] Maya Chen: We'll do canary hedging: 20% kernel A->B, monitor p50/p99, if <5% regressions we open to 50%.
[06:58] Mark Dawson: Also add latency trace correlation to user IDs so we can see impact on real query patterns.
[07:05] Maya Chen: We'll add that to the trace instrumentation.
[07:10] Ethan Brooks: Quick housekeeping — two requests from legal: data residency for logs, and contract appendix for retention. I'll get legal to send a standard appendix.
[07:20] Ravi Kumar: Cool. Also, any competitor risk if we switch to Anthropic? We had internal discussions.
[07:27] Ethan Brooks: We support multiple model backends in the catalog. If you want a multi-provider hedging strategy we can propose a routing policy. But that complicates caching since different models won't share KV.
[07:40] Mark Dawson: Noted. For now we want to keep a single model family to preserve cache advantages.
[07:46] Maya Chen: One more perf data point — streaming handshake latency contributed ~40ms in average for first chunk in our test because the client did a 3-way SSE handshake. We recommended that clients send the first chunk early and keep the connection warm.
[07:59] Lina Ortega: We'll check if our front-end can pre-open persistent connections for heavy customers.
[08:06] Ethan Brooks: Ok summary: Maya to push JMeter script and v3 benchmark. Mark to upload seqlen hist and prompts. Lina to share VPC/firewall. Ethan to push pricing and SOC2/docs. Next sync 01/26.
[08:22] Ravi Kumar: Thanks all. Quick micro question — if the microburst shows 25% TTFT improvement is there a path to shorten pilot lead time?
[08:30] Ethan Brooks: Yes we'll fast track a pilot expansion and optionally offer a short-term service credit to offset migration ops. I'll outline details in the follow-up email.
[08:40] [end of meeting]
Notes: Some stutters and mis-words in transcript (auto-transcribe) — e.g., "KV cache" sometimes as "K V cash", "fwd-opt" as "ford opt". Attached artifacts: bench sheet v2 (link), SOC2 playbook (link), microburst plan draft (link).
